# Dyeing with mordants and vat dyes (`mordant_dyeing`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by textile_fibres, alkali_soda, acids_bases_ph
- Core idea: Most plant dyes wash out unless the fibre is first treated with a mordant, a metal salt that binds dye to fibre. Simmer wool for an hour with alum (about a quarter of the wool's weight, often with a little tartar), then in the dye bath: madder root gives red, weld yellow; iron salts sadden colours towards black. Indigo and woad work differently: the blue is insoluble, so it is made soluble in a warm alkaline, fermenting vat (stale urine or lime with bran), the cloth comes out yellow-green and turns blue in the air. Wool and silk take dyes easily; linen and cotton are much harder.
- Pitfalls:
  - Dyeing without a mordant, or on greasy, unscoured wool; the colour runs.
  - Boiling madder; above about 70 °C the red turns brown.
  - Stirring air into the indigo vat, which spoils it.
  - Too much iron or alum makes fibres brittle; alum polluted with iron dulls every colour.
  - Expecting one recipe for all fibres; cotton needs tannin and oil treatments (Turkey red took weeks).
- History: india: c. 2000 BC – madder-dyed, mordanted cotton at Mohenjo-daro; India is the classical home of indigo and of printed, mordant-dyed cottons; americas: c. 4000 BC – indigo-dyed cotton at Huaca Prieta, Peru, the oldest known; cochineal red in Peru and Mexico from the 1st millennium BC; egypt: c. 2000 BC – madder and indigotin on linen; Pliny describes Egyptian mordant dyeing in the 1st c. AD; mesopotamia: c. 1500 BC – shellfish purple on the Levantine coast (earlier in Minoan Crete); alum in cuneiform dye recipes; china: by c. 1000 BC – indigo, madder and gardenia on silk; mordants named in Zhou texts; europe: medieval woad, madder, kermes; 1462 alum found at Tolfa and made a papal monopoly; 1548 Rosetti's Plictho, the first printed dye book
- Read:
  - Gioanventura Rosetti, Plictho de l'arte de' tentori (1548)
  - Dominique Cardon, Natural Dyes: Sources, Tradition, Technology and Science (2007)
  - Jeffrey C. Splitstoser et al., Early pre-Hispanic use of indigo blue in Peru, Science Advances 2 (2016)
